chunks: And what Musa ibn al-Qasim narrated from Ibn Abi Umayr from Sayf al-Tammarr, who said:

I said to Abu Abdillah (peace be upon him): 'It has reached us that during that year, when we were walking from you, you said regarding riding.' He said: 'People perform Hajj by walking and by riding.' I said: 'I am not asking you about this.' He said: 'About what do you ask me?' I said: 'What is more beloved to you, that we walk or that we ride?' He said: 'Riding is more beloved to me, for that is stronger for supplication and worship.'

Thus, the ruling in these narrations is that whoever is strong for walking, and this does not weaken him from supplication and rituals, or whoever has his load carried with him, if he becomes weary he rides; for walking is superior to riding for him. And whoever is weakened by walking, and does not have with him what he can resort to for riding when he becomes weary, then it is not permissible for him to depart except as a rider.
And indicating to this meaning is what Musa ibn al-Qasim narrated from Safwan from Abdullah ibn Bukayr, who said:

I said to Abu Abdillah (peace be upon him): 'We intend to depart for Mecca.' He said: 'Do not walk, but ride.' I said: 'May God perfect you, it has reached us that Hasan ibn Ali (peace be upon him) performed Hajj twenty times on foot.' He said: 'Indeed, Hasan ibn Ali (peace be upon him) used to walk, and his loads and beasts of burden were carried with him.'

It is also possible that he preferred riding over walking only when he knew that he would reach Mecca if he rode before the walkers, so he would worship God Almighty and increase in prayer until the walkers arrived.

key_terms.الرُّكُوب: Riding (traveling on beasts of burden or vehicles)
key_terms.الْمَشَّاءُونَ: The walkers (those performing Hajj on foot)

ai.seo_question: What is the Islamic ruling on walking versus riding during Hajj according to the Imams?
ai.summary: This narration from *Tahdhib al-Ahkam* clarifies the juristic preference for riding during Hajj by emphasizing the preservation of physical strength for *du'a* and *ibadah*, a principle derived from Imam al-Sadiq's (AS) response to Musa ibn al-Qasim. The text further contextualizes the practice of Imam al-Hasan (AS), noting that his walking was accompanied by carried loads, distinguishing his case from those who must walk without support, thereby establishing a nuanced legal framework for varying levels of physical capability and resource availability.
